column3: Immediate antecedent: the owner turns abundant fruit into a boast of superior wealth and followers.
The nearby command to recite frames the passage but does not clarify divine will or strength in the admonition.
Its concern for vulnerable offspring gives only a secondary counterweight to boasting in children.
Directly limits human benefit and harm to what Allah wills, closely echoing the focus's attribution of power.
Immediate outcome: neither a supporting group nor the owner himself can help apart from Allah.
Affirms Allah as the truly Strong and Mighty, grounding the correction that no strength exists independently of Him.
A disbeliever's confident claim of future wealth and children closely parallels the focus's wealth-and-offspring contrast.
Its warning against worldly adornment prepares the nearby contrast with wealth-centered pride.
Human strength and trustworthiness in hiring do not address the source or dependence of the garden owner's power.
Condemns the collector who counts accumulated wealth, a related posture of confidence in possessions.
Immediate antecedent: the owner enters the garden unjust to himself and declares it imperishable.
Moses' announcement of messengerhood has no substantive link to the focus's correction of wealth and power.
Noah's refusal of payment and reliance on Allah are a distant contrast to material status.
The nearby choice between belief and disbelief supplies the moral frame for the ensuing parable.
Its denial of any strength or helper supports the focus's rejection of independent human power.
The shared rebuke formula and instruction to speak rightly concern slander, not wealth or divine dependence.
Immediate antecedent: the owner adds denial of the Hour and confidence in a better return to his worldly presumption.
The warning against ascribing a child to Allah does not clarify the focus's mention of human children as status.
Allah's statement that He granted extended wealth challenges treating wealth as self-originating.
The promise not to waste righteous work is a nearby value contrast but does not explain the admonition.
Allah's sufficiency for believers and His strength offer a broad parallel to power belonging to Him.
Jacob's restored sight does not illuminate the relation between wealth, will, and power.
Immediate conclusion: all true authority, reward, and outcome belong to Allah.
Immediate antecedent: the companion recalls the owner's created origin to undermine his self-exalting claim.
The garden owners are reproved for failing to glorify Allah, closely paralleling the focus's prescribed response on entering a garden.
Lasting gardens as reward form the nearby contrast to the insecure worldly garden.
A creature's assertion of strength is only a distant contrast to the focus's denial of independent strength.
The temptation of internal betrayal does not clarify possession, divine will, or power.
Immediate setup: Allah gives one man two gardens, establishing the provision later misread as personal superiority.
Allah provides for whom He wills and is Strong and Mighty, directly joining provision, will, and divine power.
Abraham disclaims power to secure anything apart from Allah and places reliance in Him.
Immediate outcome: ruin makes the owner regret associating anyone with his Lord.
Treating wealth as a means of sustenance offers only an indirect corrective to proud ownership.
Rejecting false association with Allah is thematically related but outside the focus's wealth-and-power setting.
Immediate setup: the gardens' full yield and river are presented as given abundance before the owner's boast.
Travel fatigue in Moses' journey has no useful connection to the focus.
Jesus' obedience and Allah's watchfulness provide only a broad contrast to autonomous human agency.
Immediate antecedent: the companion declares Allah alone his Lord and rejects association.
Allah's strength and the provision of useful iron broadly support the distinction between granted means and divine power.
Mutual enjoyment between jinn and humans does not clarify the garden admonition.
The damaged boat episode concerns hidden wisdom, not wealth or attribution of power.
Immediate continuation: the companion attributes better provision and the garden's possible destruction to his Lord.
Allah's strength in seizing deniers offers a broad warning against ignoring the stronger divine power.
'Who is stronger than us?' is answered by the Creator's greater strength, directly countering self-confident power claims.
Fire as reminder and benefit for travelers does not illuminate the focus.
Mary's appeal for protection does not address the source of wealth or strength.
Insincere profession of belief has no specific relation to the garden owner's claim.
The correction about patience in Moses' journey is unrelated to the focus.
It explicitly assigns all power to Allah, a direct doctrinal counterpart to 'no strength except through Allah.'
The earlier correction about patience in Moses' journey is unrelated to the focus.
Moses' request for leniency after forgetfulness does not clarify the focus.
The warning against following Satan into disbelief is only a broad counterpart to the owner's self-wronging.
Allah alone is the Provider and Possessor of firm strength, directly joining the focus's two central claims.
Divine steadfastening of the Prophet is a remote instance of dependence on Allah.
Taking the covenant with strength concerns obedient resolve, not the source of power or wealth.
The fulfilled vision is expressly conditioned by Allah's will, a concise verbal parallel to the focus.
Its command to worship Allah without association reinforces the companion's rejection of assigning divine partnership.
The dispute among peoples in Hell does not illuminate the focus's warning about worldly confidence.
Shu'ayb's call to reverence has no distinct connection to the focus.
Allah's knowledge of the unseen does not clarify wealth, will, or strength here.
Strength in holding the covenant is not the kind of power corrected in the focus.
The believers' lack of travel resources does not clarify the garden owner's claim.
The critique of unsupported speech about Allah having a child does not illuminate human wealth and offspring here.
The image of undoing spun strength is a distant warning that established capacity can be wasted.
The counselors' military strength is a limited contrast to the focus's denial of autonomous power.
A ruler granted dominion claims life-and-death power until Allah's decisive agency exposes the claim.
Lot's request for help against corrupters does not clarify the focus.
Its conditional appeal to the Lord's will occurs in a rejection of messengers and offers little interpretive support.
Speculation about the sleepers' number does not illuminate the garden admonition.
Earlier peoples had greater strength, wealth, and children yet lost, closely countering confidence in these assets.
Strength in holding the Book concerns steadfast obedience, not the focus's source-of-power claim.
Divinely decreed exile is only a distant example of outcomes determined beyond human control.
The Lord's greeting of peace has no relevant relation to the focus.
The statement that events would not occur except by Allah's will provides a broad parallel to the focus's wording.
Allah's promised victory and explicit strength broadly reinforce that ultimate power belongs to Him.
Faithful humility and reward do not clarify the focus's correction of material self-confidence.
Allah's protection and promised support, with His strength, provide a general divine-power parallel.
Creation as a test of deeds is a broad frame for treating worldly abundance as trial.
The description of a being of mighty powers is only a secondary contrast to the focus's exclusive source of strength.
Divine aid and gardens for believers connect only indirectly through support and descendants.
The repeated greeting of peace does not illuminate the focus.
The decree concerning Hell has no useful connection to the garden admonition.
The accusation against Moses has no relation to wealth, will, or strength in the focus.
Its lavish silver houses for disbelievers show that visible affluence is not a sign of independent worth or favor.
Stronger towns are destroyed with no helper, a broad counterpart to confidence in strength.
Sudden punishment at an appointed term only distantly parallels the threatened sudden ruin of the garden.
The prayer for forgiveness and mercy does not clarify the focus.
Jesus asks Allah for provision and names Him the best provider, countering self-sufficient possession.
Former peoples were stronger and more productive yet ruined through self-wronging, a broad warning against proud capacity.
The command to prepare military strength does not address its divine source or the focus's moral correction.
The mature believer thanks Allah for blessings to himself, parents, and offspring, contrasting boastful reliance on children.
The accusation of being approached from the right has no relevant connection.
The Prophet's marital permissions do not illuminate the focus.
The confession of neglecting prayer has no specific relation to wealth or divine power.
The exception for Allah's devoted servants supplies no distinct interpretive link.
Recognition of the Day of Recompense does not clarify the focus.
Seeking Allah's bounty and the greater return of good deeds offer a distant corrective to worldly self-reliance.
The magicians' oath by Pharaoh's might provides a contrast case of attributing victory to created power.
Allah's knowledge of what people conceal does not clarify the focus.
Dhu al-Qarnayn's coordinated construction is nearby but does not explain the garden owner's dependence on Allah.
Immediate continuation: the garden's water may sink beyond recovery, making its owner powerless to restore it.
The rain-fed vegetation that becomes scattered debris directly extends the lesson that worldly flourishing is transient.
Wealth and children are called worldly adornment, while enduring righteous works are better with Allah, directly interpreting the focus's contrast.
Allah gives and removes dominion, honors and humiliates, and holds all good in His hand, directly locating power in Him.
If Allah helps none can overcome, and if He forsakes none can help, closely echoing the focus's dependence claim.
Only Allah can remove harm or bestow good, directly denying independent efficacy to possessions or persons.
Victory is only from Allah, a direct parallel to treating effective strength as divine rather than autonomous.
Human action is explicitly attributed to Allah's effective agency, closely supporting the focus's correction of self-attributed power.
Nothing befalls except what Allah has decreed; He is the believers' protector, strongly grounding reliance beyond visible assets.
Worldly growth becomes dry debris by Allah's command, a close parallel to the garden's threatened sudden ruin.
The questions about who provides and controls life direct recognition of sustaining power to Allah.
No one can remove Allah's harm or repel His bounty, directly denying the protective force of wealth and followers.
Jacob states that judgment belongs only to Allah and places his trust in Him, a close dependence parallel.
Jacob's precaution could not avail against Allah's decree, qualifying confidence in human means.
When Allah wills harm for a people none can repel it or protect them, directly paralleling the garden's possible loss.
Allah expands and restricts provision, while worldly life is brief, jointly correcting confidence in abundance.
Messengers say Allah favors whom He wills and command reliance on Him, linking divine will with human dependence.
Allah causes crops, palms, grapes, and every fruit to grow, directly assigning garden fertility to divine agency.
Every blessing is from Allah, a concise corrective to treating material abundance as self-owned.
A secure, well-provisioned town loses its blessings through ingratitude, a broad garden-like warning.
Allah expands and restricts provision for whom He wills, directly qualifying status based on wealth.
Allah has no partner in dominion and no protector from weakness; magnifying Him directly reinforces the focus's theology of power.
Worldly splendor is identified as a test and Allah's provision as better and more lasting.
It asks whether wealth and sons mean that good is being hastened to their owners, directly challenging that inference.
The following denial makes clear that material abundance is not evidence of privileged favor.
The recipient of extraordinary power calls it a bounty from his Lord and a test of gratitude, a close model for the speech required in 18:39.
Allah's bounty toward people is stated alongside their frequent ingratitude, broadly reinforcing the required acknowledgment.
Qarun attributes his wealth to personal knowledge, a direct counterpart to the garden owner's self-attribution.
Qarun and his house are swallowed by the earth, closely paralleling the sudden collapse of apparently secure wealth.
Observers recognize that Allah expands and restricts provision, explicitly reversing envy of Qarun's abundance.
Allah expands and restricts provision for whom He wills, directly qualifying material superiority.
The expansion and restriction of provision are signs for believers, a related corrective to possession-based judgment.
The people of Sab'a receive two gardens and are commanded to eat from their Lord's provision and give thanks, closely paralleling the focus.
Sab'a's grateful-garden provision is replaced after turning away, a close warning about the loss of granted abundance.
Greater wealth and children are explicitly denied as a measure of nearness to Allah.
Allah expands and restricts provision and replaces what is spent, reinforcing His control over wealth.
It asks whether any creator besides Allah provides from heaven and earth, directly locating provision's source.
Created objects cannot prevent Allah's intended harm or withhold His mercy, directly denying independent protective power.
A person claims wealth was given because of personal knowledge, but Allah calls it a test, closely paralleling proud self-attribution.
Allah expands and restricts provision, a direct counterpoint to equating abundance with autonomous strength.
The man's confidence that he will receive good even on return to his Lord closely resembles the garden owner's presumption in 18:36.
The treasures of the heavens and earth belong to Allah, who expands and restricts provision as He wills.
Provision is measured out lest people transgress, directly qualifying the moral meaning of abundance.
Allah distributes worldly livelihood and raises some above others in rank, undermining claims of self-produced status.
All such luxury is only enjoyment of worldly life, a close value contrast to material display.
Allah is self-sufficient while people are needy, directly opposing the posture of material self-sufficiency.
Worldly life is rivalry in wealth and children followed by fading growth, closely matching the focus's warning.
Believers are told not to exult over what they have been given, directly countering boastful possession.
Wealth and children must not distract from Allah's remembrance, directly supplying the focus's corrective orientation.
Wealth and children are a trial, directly reframing the assets invoked in 18:39.
Allah provides an exit and sustenance from unforeseen sources for the God-conscious, countering reliance on visible means.
Whoever relies on Allah finds Him sufficient; Allah's command reaches its measure, closely expressing the focus's dependence.
The owners of a garden are tested as they plan to harvest it, a direct narrative parallel to the garden setting.
A visitation from the Lord strikes the garden overnight, closely paralleling the threatened destructive reckoning in 18:40.
After their garden's loss, the owners hope their Lord will replace it with something better, echoing the companion's appeal in 18:40.
Human willing is explicitly dependent on Allah's will, directly supporting 'what Allah wills.'
Human willing occurs only if Allah, Lord of the worlds, wills, another direct formulation of the focus's principle.
Love of children and amassed wealth is named as worldly adornment, a close frame for the focus's status contrast.
Believers are directed not to covet others' advantages but to ask Allah of His bounty, countering comparative material pride.
The giver of gardens commands grateful, measured use of their yield and warns against excess.
Faith and reverence open blessings from heaven and earth, locating prosperity in Allah rather than self-sufficiency.
Love of relatives, wealth, and trade above Allah is directly censured, providing a sharp priority contrast to boasting in wealth and children.
Wealth and children are not to be admired; Allah uses them as a trial and punishment in worldly life.
The repeated warning that wealth and children may be a means of punishment reinforces their nonprivileged status.
Allah's differing provision is presented as His favor, while its denial is condemned, directly opposing ungrateful ownership claims.
Earthly adornment is explicitly made by Allah as a test, supplying the governing frame for the garden owner's abundance.
Allah can make the earth's adornment barren ground, directly anticipating the garden's possible destruction.
People are tested by both good and evil, a broad but direct frame for prosperity as trial.
On the Day of Judgment neither wealth nor children will avail, directly relativizing the two assets named in the focus.
No parent or child can avail another before Allah, a related limit on the protective value of family ties.
Wealth and children do not bring people near to Allah; only faith and righteous work do, directly answering the focus's comparison.
The yield of divinely made gardens is followed by a call to gratitude, a close provision-and-thankfulness parallel.
Worldly life is diversion and play, while piety prevents loss of reward; wealth is not the enduring measure.
Every calamity is recorded before it occurs, directly qualifying the owner's confidence that his garden cannot perish.
The person who receives bounty says his Lord has honored him, a direct analogue to reading prosperity as personal standing.
The person who receives restricted provision says his Lord has humiliated him, completing the correction of material measures of worth.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts people, directly naming the posture behind comparative wealth claims.
This rivalry persists until the grave, reinforcing the focus's warning against enduring confidence in possessions.
Wealth and earned gains do not avail their owner, a concise direct counterpoint to reliance on material resources.
